old: The inner child won’t trust you because you said three kind sentences during one meditation. Trust grows when the present-day adult becomes reliable.
new: Your inner child won’t trust you right away. It’s not going to be enough for you to meditate, say three nice sentences to the inner child and expect to have its trust. What’s going to help your inner child to trust you is you, as a person that you are right now.

old: I organize that adult capacity into three functions: Nurturer, Protector, and Leader/Guru. They aren’t three literal beings. They’re three ways the present-day person reparents the inner child.
new: In this post I am going to talk about what you need to develop in yourself in order to be able to reparent your inner child. I’m going to talk about it in terms of three aspects: your Nurturer, your Protector and your Leader/Guru, but I don’t mean them as if there were really three people in you. It’s you that needs to develop these qualities.

old: The child’s worth doesn’t depend on developing those capacities. Worth was never the missing skill. The child also brings play, tenderness, irreverence, creativity, and wonder. Those qualities belong inside the adult relationship, not just the wounds.
new: Also, your inner child’s worth is not dependent on these qualities… It has its own worth, and its own qualities, like playing, being tender, not taking life too seriously, being creative and wondering at the world.

old: Some people can summon one of those adult functions. Others go blank, hear only the inherited critic, or feel like a child pretending to be grown. Telling them to “be the adult” assumes the capacity they are trying to build.
new: The problem is, that some people do not have access to their adult functions at will. Instead, they may go blank, access an inherited inner critic, or even more commonly – access a child part who may be playing at being an adult. Telling them to just access their adult is like telling them to just be able to fly.

old: For that starting point, I use a provisional, author-developed bridge I call borrowed adulthood. It combines familiar practices—witnessing, modeling, supported action, and gradual transfer of responsibility—without claiming that the complete sequence has been validated as one treatment.
new: To help these people access their adult functions, I recommend the following steps. Please note, the following is a bridge that I developed – while many of the steps have been shown to be effective, the entirety of the steps have not (to the best of my knowledge).

old: Witness, when needed. Notice what is present without demanding warmth, wisdom, or certainty. If you already distinguish the internal positions, move to the adult function you need.
new: - Access a witnessing position, if necessary. If you already know how to distinguish your internal positions, skip to the next step and access the adult position you need.

old: Borrow one function. Choose a safe adult, mentor, older sibling, future self, spiritual figure, value, or written plan. Borrow only the warmth, boundary, or direction needed now.
new: - Borrow an adult function. You may “borrow” this from a safe adult in your life, a mentor, an older sibling, a future version of yourself, a spiritual figure, a value, or even a written plan. Borrow whatever you need – warmth, direction, etc.

old: Become the adult apprentice. Choose the exact words or action yourself and carry at least one small part.
new: - Put on the adult hat as an apprentice. Now, in this position, figure out what you would want to say or do – and then do at least a part of that.

old: Hand it back. Name what the borrowed figure modeled and what five percent you can now do without them.
new: - Return the adult hat, noticing what you borrowed and what you were able to do on your own (even if it’s only 5%).

old: The borrowed figure stays beside your judgment rather than replacing it. The fuller sequence is in my Inner Child Self-Love Reparenting Guide.
new: This is a borrowed figure, so you’re still making the choice. The longer version of this exercise can be found in my Inner Child Self-Love Reparenting Guide .

old: You don’t need a history full of trustworthy people to borrow care. Use a remembered person when that helps, or an imagined adult whose intention is to take good care of you. Ask, “What would that person say or do with my actual history, limitations, and options?” Begin with the least cruel response you can believe if warmth is unavailable. Once you find one usable sentence or action, try it rather than repeating the exercise in different words.
new: You don’t have to have trustworthy people in your history. Just imagine a good adult. See if you can imagine what they would say/do in your situation, with your history, limitations, options, etc. If you can’t imagine good, imagine the least cruel thing you can. Once you’ve found something good, try it, don’t keep doing the exercise.

old: Borrowing can also help the position trying to be the adult: how would a decent adult hear distrust without retaliating, defending their goodness, collapsing, or leaving? Borrow that one response. You may still feel young while doing it; adult identity can develop after the behavior.
new: It can be helpful to use borrowing when you’re in the adult position and not knowing what a decent adult would do, especially when it seems like any response will be retaliatory, defensive, collapsing, leaving, etc. Borrow a decent adult’s response. You may still feel young when you do it, it’s okay, you’ll become an adult after you act like one.

old: Letting a younger feeling-state speak doesn’t mean handing adult judgment to an outside caretaker or trying to become literally younger. Wonder, play, vivid sensation, vulnerability, honest need, or the wish to carry fewer decisions can all come forward while the internal adult remains present.
new: It is possible to regress psychologically and allow those younger states to talk, but still maintain adult judgement. You don't have to turn that judgement over to someone else or literally become younger. You just get to tap into those feelings of wonder, play, sensation, vulnerability, need or whatever it is you feel you need less responsibility.

old: “A younger part of me may speak. The adult in me remains here to listen, evaluate, protect, and stop. No child-state, guide, recording, or outside person replaces adult judgment.”
new: "It is okay for a younger part of me to talk. But I understand that the adult in me is always going to be here, evaluating, protecting me and stopping me if needed. I am not going to replace my adult judgement with any child state, guide, recording or person."

old: That distinction lets you recover curiosity, spontaneity, play, sensory freshness, honest need, and quick emotional movement without pairing those gifts with obedience, helplessness, scolding, or weakened judgment.
new: This way you get the benefits of being young; curiosity, spontaneity, play, sensation, the ability to state your needs, to feel easily etc without any of the negatives of being a child, like obeying, being helpless, being scolded, the lack of good judgement etc.

old: When love is available, the younger state doesn’t have to believe in it before you can offer it. Trust can question your promises, remember failures of protection, and take its time. Love can remain present while that happens.
new: If the younger position doesn’t believe you love him/her yet, you can still love him/her. You can love him/her even if the trust position doesn’t trust your promises yet, even if he/she remembers that you haven’t been able to protect him/her yet.

old: “Okay. I believe that you don’t believe me. I still love you. You don’t have to love me back. Tell me what feels unsafe.”
new: You can start with something like, “Okay. I believe that you don’t believe me. I still love you though. It’s okay if you don’t love me yet. Tell me what doesn’t feel safe to you.”

old: That isn’t a way to end the complaint. Listen for what is true in it and answer seriously. Hearing anger without retaliation, admitting a real failure, and repairing after an internal attack are evidence alongside meals, boundaries, appointments, and kept promises. Non-retaliation expresses love; it shouldn’t replace love with a colder performance of good behavior.
new: Respond to complaints by hearing the truth in them and by responding to them, as well as by providing the other evidence of love: preparing and serving meals, setting limits to protect him/her, taking him/her to appointments, keeping promises, admitting when you haven’t been able to live up to your promises, etc. If the younger position attacks you in his/her mind, admit that you haven’t been able to protect him/her yet, work on it, and let him/her know when you’ve made a change. Show your love by not retaliating, but don’t substitute not retaliating for loving the younger position.

old: Notice what each position teaches the others. A vow followed by blame when it is doubted teaches that love depends on receiving it correctly. The blaming voice and the voice making the vow may be different positions, the same position, or a blend. Don’t decide from the person’s chronological age.
new: Keep in mind that the position that made the vow and the position that blames the child for not accepting the vow may be two separate positions, or they may be the same position, or they may be a blend. Don’t go by chronological age.

old: When a younger version of you becomes the defendant, ask what they understood then, what options they could see and tolerate, and what happened because of the choice. Harm can require responsibility and repair. Punishment cannot retroactively create the capacity that was missing.
new: Imagine that you are in court and the defendant is you, only a few years younger. Would it be of any value to try and understand why you did whatever it was you did? Would it help to try and appreciate what options you felt you had? Would any useful insight be gained by considering the consequences of your actions? Whilst acknowledging the harm you may have caused, and working to address and repair that harm, would simply punishing you make any difference to the person you were when you committed the offence?

old: Place one hand at the center of the chest as a physical connection to love. Put the other at the solar plexus, just beneath the chest, where you can relate to the vulnerable child.
new: So here is a simple easy little bit of body work that will help you get in touch with your inner child. All you have to do is place one hand in the center of your chest. Remember your heart is there and it's full of love. Now place your other hand just below that, at your solar plexis, that is where you can relate to your child.

old: Send warmth from the heart toward the child. Notice whatever comes back—a sensation, image, feeling, resistance, or nothing—and answer with warmth again. Let it become a conversation rather than a performance.
new: Now begin sending love down to your child from your heart and just notice what comes up for you. It doesn't matter if something comes up or not, if there is resistance come it with love, if you feel or see something come it with love. Just communicate with your child from your heart.

old: Love above. Child below. Adult present.
new: Now remember when you do this, Love is on top and your child is on the bottom and you as the adult are right there with them.

old: The Nurturer brings warmth without trying to rush the feeling away, and takes pleasure in the child’s company: “I’m glad you’re here.” The child needs to be enjoyed, not only comforted when hurt.
“It’s okay to feel this.” “I’m here.” “You don’t have to do anything right now.” “You are not too much.” “You can be small here.” “You can be angry here.” “You can be sad here.” “I will stay.”
new: One of the most important things you can do as a Nurturer is to enjoy your children. To sit back and not feel like you have to move their feelings, but actually say to them, “I’m really glad you are here in this moment.” Children need to be enjoyed, not just consoled when they are hurt.
“I know it’s okay for you to feel the way you are feeling.”
“I want you to know that I’m here for you.”
“Right now, you don’t have to do anything.”
“You are not too much.”
“It’s okay to be small. You can be small here with me.”
“It’s okay to be angry. You can be angry here.”
“It’s okay to be sad. You can be sad here.”
“I’m going to be here for you.”

old: The Protector turns warmth into something the child can believe.
new: Identify your protector and try to bring a bit of their warmth.

old: “I will set the boundary.” “I will leave the unsafe conversation.” “I will stop texting the person who destabilizes us.” “I will eat.” “I will sleep.” “I will keep a small promise.” “I will not leave the child alone with adult consequences.”
new: Then set boundaries together - it can be anything from, 'I will leave that conversation', 'I will stop texting that person', 'I will eat today', 'I will get some sleep tonight', 'I will do x', or, 'I won't put you in the position of having to deal with x '.

old: This is where inner-child practice often turns decorative. The voice says loving things while the adult sends the destabilizing message, skips the meal, avoids the task, and breaks the promise. Trust begins when you handle the consequence.
new: It's important to note that lots of people do ICW but it's often fluffy brouhaha - they talk to their IC, but they don't actually do the things they need to in their adult life. So in order to build trust with your IC, you need to do the thing . And deal with the fallout if you don't.

old: If warmth is unavailable, a protective act can begin the relationship. Make it small enough to carry out and review what actually happened. A missed action might reflect fear, exhaustion, missing skills, a practical barrier, or a poor plan. Completion without immediate relief isn’t automatically failure, and a tick on a list doesn’t prove the action helped.
new: If you can't bring any warmth to the Protector, that's okay, just work with them on doing protective things for your child. Make sure they are attainable. If you don't do them, work out why - was it fear, exhaustion, lack of skills, lack of X, poor planning, etc.? Also, make sure that doing them is actually helpful - don't just be ticking things off a list.

old: The Leader gives direction. You can call this function Leader, Guide, Guru, Wise One, Sage, Inner Teacher, Director, or Higher Adult. The label matters much less than the ability to orient the whole system toward a life.
new: Working with the Leader function, who provides direction. You can give it the name you like: Leader, Guide, Guru, Wise One, Sage, Inner Teacher, Director, Higher Adult, etc.

old: Direction can ask for something difficult without turning life into perfect discipline and hidden needs. Sometimes the next adult move is asking for help, expressing a preference, or letting a safe person see an imperfection. Wanting closeness is legitimate; punishing someone for needing space is a different strategy. Find a way to meet the need without erasing either person.
new: Invite it to give direction in an effective way, not in a way that expects you to be perfectly disciplined and not have any needs. Ask it to help you find a way to do the adult thing and ask for help, express a preference, allow a safe person to see your imperfections, etc. Find ways to get your need for closeness met without punishing the other person for needing space. Etc.

old: “We are not only here to feel better.” “We are here to become whole.” “We are here to belong to life itself, not only to people who approve of us.” “We are here to serve truth, beauty, love, God, source, nature, universe, dharma, Tao, and the benefit of all beings.”
new: Affirmations to support the Leader may include: “We are not only here to feel good.” “We are here to become whole.” “We are here to belong to life itself, not only to people who approve of us.” “We are here to serve truth, beauty, love, God, source, nature, universe, dharma, Tao, the benefit of all beings.” Etc.

old: Begin with the adult function you can actually reach. Protection may come before warmth. Direction should help the child grow without erasing care, play, or support.
new: Begin working with the adult function, perhaps beginning with protection, then warmth. Be sure that the direction serves your child’s growth, but doesn’t deprive your child of necessary care, play, support, etc.

old: Use this parts language when you actually recognize a protective pattern or find it useful to explore. A sensation, distraction, or objection doesn’t establish its cause. Notice it first; hunger may need food, skepticism may be reasonable, and a sentence may simply not fit.
new: If this language is familiar to you, feel free to use it.

old: People assume inner-child work begins with the child. Very often, you meet the guard at the door first.
new: Most people assume when approaching their inner child that the first thing they’ll encounter is…their inner child.

old: You sit down to connect and get numbness, cynicism, anger, sudden hunger, a phone urge, a sexual urge, planning, sleepiness, dissociation, or the thought, “This is stupid.” I wouldn’t call those failures. They’re often the protector making an appearance in its usual charming way.
new: But more often than not, what you actually experience is numbness, cynicism, anger, hunger, the sudden urge to check your phone, a sexual urge, mental planning, sleepiness, dissociation, or the simple thought that “this is stupid”. These are all common manifestations of protectors.

old: One important voice is the inherited parent: the internalized caregiver voice formed from how the child was treated. This is different from the inner adult—the Nurturer, Protector, and Leader/Guru you deliberately build. The inherited parent may sound like a critic or warden—don’t cry, don’t be needy, don’t embarrass us, don’t become too independent—and can make a new loving voice feel fake before you’ve even begun.
new: One of the most important protectors to become aware of when approaching your inner child is your inherited parent. This is the voice of your parent(s) that you internalized as a child, based on how they treated you. This is not the same as your inner adult (Nurturer, Protector, Leader/Guru) that you will eventually build up. Often this inherited parent acts as a critic or warden, telling your inner child not to cry, not to be “needy”, not to embarrass them, not to be too independent, etc. So when you begin talking to your child in a new, loving way, this voice may jump in to say that what you’re doing is “fake”.

old: “I notice you. You are trying to protect something. I want to understand. What are you afraid would happen if you stopped?”
new: It’s okay, I see what you’re doing. Can I ask you what you’re afraid would happen if you let this go?

old: Then wait. The answer may be: “You’ll lie to yourself again.” “This will become another performance.” “If you feel the pain, you’ll be destroyed.” “You’ll use spirituality to avoid reality.” “You’ll forgive too early.” “You’ll call fantasy guidance.” “You’ll abandon us as soon as the session ends.”
new: Now be patient, and listen. It may be that they’re afraid that you’ll fall for your bullshit again, or that you’ll spiritualize this issue, or feel your pain, or forgive someone too early, or believe your fantasies again, or leave them hanging once the therapy session is over.

old: “That makes sense. You do not have to move yet. What would help you trust me 1% more?”
new: Now, thank the protective part, and ask them what they need from you to feel 1% safer.

old: Usually the protector needs evidence more than another spiritual insight. Hold the boundary. Handle the task. Eat the meal. Don’t send the message. Keep the promise. Sleep. Contact the therapist. Acknowledge the debt. Write down the truth.
new: 99% of the time, the answer will be some non-spiritual thing like maintaining a boundary, doing a certain task, eating properly, holding back from sending a text, or sleeping, or reaching out to a therapist, or acknowledging that you do, in fact, owe someone money.

old: The Protector is more than an inner voice saying no. You can practice it as a bodily sequence:
new: Does anyone here practice the following sequence to “embody” Protector?

old: Orient: look around and feel the support beneath you.
new: (1) orient self (look around, feel support, etc.),

old: Assess: ask what is known, what is uncertain, and what needs checking.
new: (2) assess situation (what do you know, not know, need to check out?),

old: Distinguish: separate present danger from uncertainty, old alarm, or imagined danger.
new: (3) differentiate between actual/real dangers, uncertainty, past dangers or imagined dangers,

old: Set one proportionate boundary: move, stop, delay, ask, leave, or get support.
new: (4) set boundaries (just one, proportional to danger level; move, stop, delay, ask, leave, get support, etc.),

old: Verify enough safety: not perfect certainty, just enough reality-based evidence for the next step.
new: (5) verify sufficient safety (based on reality), and finally

old: Stand down and rest: protection includes ending the scan when continued vigilance is no longer helping.
new: (6) stand down and rest.

old: A mature Protector can say, “I don’t know.” It can ask another human, delay interpretation, or choose a no-trance practice. I’m aiming for discernment that acts when needed and then quits scanning the room after the danger has passed.
new: Seems to me that this would be a “mature” Protector. For example, it wouldn’t be afraid to say, “I don’t know”, or to ask another human being, or to delay interpreting what’s going on, or to use a no-trance practice. I want to be able to “do” this. I am learning discernment and to quit scanning the room after taking appropriate action.

old: I connect my reparenting therapy to self-hypnosis because I find they are a perfect match. The child may arrive as an age, image, posture, voice, memory, emotion, or plain vulnerability. Sometimes no child appears. Stay with a recognizable protector, or with the sensation, feeling, or preference that is actually present.
new: Client, I want to talk about the connection between the reparenting therapy you are doing, and the self hypnosis. I think it can be a perfect fit. So, while you are in hypnosis, you might summon the child (this can be any age, image, posture, voice, memory, emotion, vulnerable self, or no child at all. If there is no child, just work with whatever protector you do have, either in the form of a sensation, feeling, or preference).

old: When the child does appear, resist the urge to begin a healing project immediately. Be with them first.
new: If there is a child that appears, don’t feel like you have to do anything with them. Just be with them.

old: “Little one, I am here. You do not have to explain everything. You do not have to be healed today. You do not have to become impressive. I only want to know what would help you feel less alone.”
new: See if you can tell the child: “Little one, you don’t have to do anything for me, you don’t have to tell me anything, you don’t even have to be healed. You don’t have to impress me. Just tell me if there’s something you need to help you feel less alone in this world.

old: The need may be warmth, play, protection, grief, anger, food, rest, a boundary, a safer relationship, less fantasy, less overwork, or one adult promise kept today.
new: It can be anything. Need to warm yourself by a fire? need to play? need protection? need to grieve? need to be angry? need food? rest? a boundary? a relationship? need to stop fantasizing? need to stop working so hard? need me to keep a promise to you for one day?

old: When a younger state, protector, feeling, or bodily signal needs care, move patiently:
Prepare: create enough time, privacy, support, and adult capacity.
Inspect: notice what is present before deciding what it means.
Ask permission: “May I come closer, or would you prefer warmth, space, words, silence, or no contact?”
Respond to one need: do the smallest useful thing rather than attempting a total repair.
Wait: let the response settle. Some changes need quiet, sleep, or ordinary time.
Reconnect: invite contact only where it is welcome. No part has to merge, disappear, forgive, or become cheerful.
Rest: stop before care becomes another performance.
Reassess: return later and ask what actually helped.

The goal isn’t “good as new,” as though history should disappear. Aim for good as you: more supported and connected while still recognizably yourself. If parts language makes you feel more divided, use signals, feelings, younger states, or another metaphor that helps.
new: Find a younger you /protector/feeling/signal in your body that needs tending to and then:
Prepare yourself to do the tending (Get yourself into a place where you have time, privacy, support etc. Be as adult as you can)
Ask for permission to move closer or what is needed (warmth, space, words, silence, no contact etc)
Do something to meet one of the needs you find when you move closer. Don’t try to fix it all.
Wait a while for the effect of what you have done to sink in.
Reconnect with that part of you ( don’t expect it to become one with you, go away, or be happy, just connect if it wants to)
Rest a while and then reassess to see how things are now.

Your aim is not to make it all good as new but good as you. Feel free to change the language if the part talk is not useful, think signal, feeling, younger you or anything that helps you connect with the issue

old: Reparenting doesn’t have to become solemn. A younger state may respond to texture, drawing, movement, a plushie with a voice, or whatever feels interesting. Keep reality-testing intact. You’re recovering play, not becoming somebody’s child, pet, doll, or owned object.
new: It is important for reparenting to remember to have fun. It's really okay to let your younger states enjoy playing with things that interest them. Touch textures, draw, move your body, talk to your plushie in a different voice, as long as you can keep reality testing intact and remember that you are not actually a child/pet/doll/whatever and are not owned, it's okay to recover your play ability.

old: Rest also doesn’t require helplessness. Reduce decisions for a defined period, put unfinished tasks somewhere visible, and let the internal adult keep watch. You remain able to move, stop, and return.
new: Resting without being helpless Sometimes you just need to rest, but you don't… [...]

old: When speech or visualization feels fake, write. Let the non-dominant hand speak for the child or protector, awkward handwriting and all. Answer with the dominant hand as the adult.
Non-dominant hand: “I don’t trust you.”
Dominant hand: “I hear that you don’t trust me. I still love you. Tell me where I’ve let you down. I won’t demand trust; I’ll listen and keep one small promise today.”
Non-dominant hand: “Which promise?”
Dominant hand: “I will eat, clean the desk, and not text the person who makes us feel unsafe.”
new: If speaking or visualization doesn’t work, try writing. Have your non-dominant hand write as your child/protector (even if your handwriting looks a little awkward), and have your dominant hand answer as you. For example, your non-dominant hand might write, “I don’t trust you.” Answer with your dominant hand, “I hear that you don’t trust me, but I love you, and I want to know where I’ve let you down. I won’t ask you to trust me, but I want to hear you out and make one promise to you that I will keep today.” Your non-dominant hand might respond, “What promise?” Your dominant hand might write, “To eat, or to clean my desk, or to not text someone who makes me feel unsafe.”

old: An induction gathers scattered attention until quieter material becomes easier to hear. You don’t have to surrender, play asleep, or obey anyone. When you’re sober, distracted, analytical, or guarded, an actual induction may help. When meditation, loveyhuasca, lucid dreaming, grief, music, prayer, fatigue, or another intense opening has already made you trancey, begin with orientation and containment instead of adding depth.
new: An induction collects up all your distracted bits and makes them quiet so that the more quiet stuff that you already have going can be heard. You don’t have to give up or go to sleep or listen to anyone. In general if you are sober, distracted, overly analytical or guarded then some actual induction can be very helpful. If you are already trancey from meditation, loveyhuasca, lucid dreaming, a period of grief, music, prayer, fatigue or anything else then you may just want to skip the induction and start with the orientation and containment.

old: Aim for the amount of trance that suits the practice: focused, warm, receptive, embodied, and still able to stop. Depth is optional.
new: A word about the depth of trance you might want to get into.

old: Prepare the session, gather attention, deepen only when that helps, then let what you notice shape the words and the next response. Counting is one way in. Conversation, story, movement, repeated sound, and curiosity can also organize attention. Say so when you use them; elegance doesn’t excuse a covert induction.
new: In general, the most effective place to begin a session is to prepare your subject, to gather their attention, and to deepen that attention if it is helpful to do so. While the most common method of gathering attention is counting, there are a number of other ways of doing so. Other methods of gathering attention include conversation, storytelling, movement, repetition, and curiosity. Whatever method you use, describe it elegantly, and don't hide your inductions.

old: For a simple, chosen target, you can test the suggestion before deepening. If the useful response is already happening, build from it. An induction helps you find a receptive way of listening; you don’t need to complete a ceremony before you’re allowed to respond.
new: Finally, it's often possible to test your suggestions, even before you do deepening, as long as the target is simple and chosen by you. The reason this works is that even the act of induction puts your subject into a

old: Choose one purpose, one starting anchor or image, and a way back. Decide whether warmth, a firm boundary, direction, or neutral witnessing would help. Floating, stairs, gardens, inner rooms, colored light, and child dialogue do not all need to report for duty at once. Switch consciously when the metaphor stops helping.
new: Make up your mind what you are doing and stick to it. You can have a purpose, a starting point, anchor, image, way back. Is this a warm exercise, a boundary, offering direction, or neutral? If it is neutral you can use many images, floating, stairs, gardens, inner place, coloured lights, talking to inner child etc. However, if you do use these, do it consciously.

old: Imagery is optional. A signal may arrive through sensation, rhythm, movement, words, spatial sense, simple knowing, or no response at all. Keep the language in the world you chose: let a count mark something meaningful there, and reverse the journey when you finish. Borrow qualities such as warmth or steadiness without replacing your identity.
new: You don’t have to use images, you can use any modality, movement, words, sense of space or simply knowing. If you count up to do something, make sure it is relevant to what you are doing and count back when you finish. If you use other qualities, don’t imply that they are you.

old: Pick one central verb, one sensory quality, one short refrain, and one transition phrase, then read the script aloud; long elegant sentences become soup during an induction.
new: Have a central verb, sense quality, refrain and transition phrase that you use consistently. Read your script out loud to check it. Long, elegant sentences read well on the page but can sound like soup when you’re trying to induce.

old: Read the induction and Come all the way back while fully awake. Choose the question or quality you want to explore, what you’re leaving alone today, and how much time you have. Love, play, confidence, creativity, and communion are worthwhile purposes; you don’t have to find a problem. Leave several minutes for returning and reflecting.
new: Read through the induction and Come all the way back to orient yourself to what will happen. Then decide what you want to explore, what you want to leave alone, and how much time you have. You may want to do the exercise for positive purposes such as stimulating love, play, confidence, creativity, or communion. Plan to allow a few minutes at the end for returning and reflecting on the experience.

old: Choose a physically secure place without driving, water, machinery, or anyone needing your supervision. When intoxicated, acutely confused, or unable to keep yourself safe, deal with immediate support rather than exploratory hypnosis. The later Already open? practice is for orientation, not permission to intensify an unstable state.
new: Make sure you are in a safe place. Don't do this exercise if you are driving, near water, working with machinery, or taking care of others. Don't do this exercise if you are under the influence of alcohol or drugs, acutely confused, or otherwise not able to take care of yourself. (The only exception is the exercise later in this section entitled "Already open?" which is designed to help orient you.)

old: Decide what kind of encouragement is welcome: spacious listening, warm company, or a firmer invitation to stay with a feeling. Preview eye closure, any repeated exit and re-entry, and the return. For a recording, read the script beforehand when possible. “Stop” ends the exercise; “less” reduces the demand; “quiet” stops the words. You can simply open your eyes and finish. No inner part has to approve your decision to stop.
new: Decide how direct you want to be encouraged to go into a hypnotic state. Read through the script to find out what is going to happen, including the fact that your eyes will be asked to close and that you may be asked to come out of the hypnotic state and then go back in again. If you are using an audio recording, it's best to read the script ahead of time. Remind yourself that you can end the exercise at any time by saying "stop" (or "less" if you want less demand to go into the hypnotic state or "quiet" if you want the talking to stop), or by opening your eyes and ending the exercise. No part of you has to give permission for you to end the exercise.

old: When entry and return are unfamiliar, first rehearse them without a difficult subject. Once you know how to change direction, you don’t need to supervise every moment. Let a useful response become easier and less effortful. A no remains no; silence doesn’t authorize a narrator to add something you haven’t agreed to.
new: Until you are confident about how to get in and out, it is wise to rehearse the skill in a context where you do not require the maximum effort that difficult subjects demand. Once the skill is easier to apply, you can relax into using it effortlessly. It is the lack of effort that produces the maximum benefit. Saying no is enough. You don’t have to say anything.

old: Let the next invitation grow from the response you got—not the response the script expected.Utilization means working with what actually happens: a thought, sound, movement, or objection may change where the practice goes. Notice what actually happens; no change doesn’t mean secret success. Keep safety and exit instructions plain. Appendix B teaches the richer language tools, and Let the next response guide you shows how to use them after the induction.
new: Develop the next part of your induction from what your subject is responding to, not what you intended. This principle of utilization means that whatever happens can be developed. If nothing happens, then nothing has happened. You don’t have to pretend that something has. The subject needs to know they are safe and how to leave the experience. The language skills that facilitate these are described in Appendix B and used in Let the next response guide you .

old: Read this slowly into a recorder, speak it aloud, or learn its movement and use silent words if that comes easily. Choose one anchor—a sound, bodily contact, or your two-hand practice—and an opening phrase. Keep using the same anchor where the words refer to it. Pause between paragraphs; don’t read the delivery directions aloud.
new: Practise reading this slowly into a recorder, or reading it aloud, or if you can learn it and use silent words. Choose to use one of the three anchors – sound, bodily contact or two hands - throughout and include the opening phrase for that practice. Whenever the words below refer to ‘the anchor’ use the one you’ve chosen. Pause for a few moments at the end of each paragraph. Don’t read aloud the instructions for how to do the reading.

old: Let your eyes settle somewhere in the room, somewhere they can rest for a little while, and notice the difference between looking for something and letting what is already there come into view.
new: As your eyes look somewhere in the room, notice the difference between looking for something and seeing what is there.

old: There is a surface beneath you. Notice where you meet it … the contact, the pressure, whatever you can actually feel. And while you notice that, a sound may reach you, or a breath may draw your attention, without needing you to arrange either one.
new: As you notice the surface beneath you, notice the feel of the contact, the pressure, the feel of it. And as you notice the anchor, perhaps a sound or the feel of the breath,

old: You can give this a little time.
new: There’s time to do this.

old: A thought about the day may still be here. A thought about whether you’re doing this properly may be here too. There is room to notice a thought and return to the anchor you chose, without finishing the thought first.
new: It might be that a thought about something that’s happened during the day is still with you, or perhaps there’s a thought about doing this properly. Whatever is there, can you find it in yourself to turn your attention back to the anchor, even if there is a thought there?

old: And as you return, you may find one detail that holds your interest … something about the sound, or the contact, or that particular way of listening … and let attention stay with it long enough to become curious.
new: and when you do come back, perhaps there was something of interest to you in all of this

old: Perhaps you can give yourself the time you would give someone you care about who has begun to speak and hasn’t yet found the words. You can remain nearby, listening, without finishing their sentence for them.
new: Perhaps you can give yourself the time that you might give to someone dear to you

old: Let your chosen phrase come to mind now. Say it as an invitation, and notice how it is received.
new: Try a phrase that you choose for yourself to see how it is for you

old: As you continue, your eyes can close, soften, or stay open. Let that be a choice you make. Listening may deepen while a sound from the room remains available in the background.
new: You can close your eyes, soften them or keep them open as you proceed

old: Count slowly from five to one. Give each number its own moment.
new: If you like, count to yourself, from 5 to 1

old: Five. Notice your chosen anchor again. Four. Let attention gather around what you find. Three. Leave a little space after the words. Two. Listen into that space, without preparing an answer. One. Stay here for a moment.
new: 5, perhaps notice again what you have chosen to be your anchor for today, 4, and notice what you notice, 3, leave some space, 2, and listen, even to the silence, 1

old: Bring your chosen concern lightly to mind, or remain with your wish for contact. Let it be present without rehearsing its whole story.
new: Now take your concern to mind very lightly, or simply hold the wish to make contact.

old: What am I noticing now?
new: What do you notice now?

old: Give the response time to take its own form. It might be a sensation, a few words, an image, a feeling, or an impulse to move. There may be nothing clear yet.
new: Wait for the response to take whatever form it will. It may be subtle and at first just a sensation, or perhaps you receive words, images, feelings, movement, or none of these at this time.

old: Leave room to notice, with words or without them.
new: Now, taking whatever form it will, words or otherwise, notice:

old: Use this when loveyhuasca, meditation, lucid dreaming, grief, music, prayer, erotic energy, exhaustion, or intense beauty has already opened the state. Stabilize before making it stronger.
new: Useful after opening a state with loveyhuasca, meditation, lucid dreaming, grief, music, prayer, erotic energy, exhaustion, or intense beauty, to first stabilize the state you’re in, before amplifying it.

old: “The state is already open. I do not need to intensify it. I need to aim it, stabilize it, and keep it kind.”
new: “I don’t need this to get more intense. I need to focus and stabilize it.”

old: Look around the room. Name where you are. Name the date, or at least the day. Feel your feet, hands, and spine. Press your thumbs gently but firmly against your index fingers. Focus on the physical friction of skin meeting skin.
new: Look around the room, and figure out where you are. What date is it? If you’re not sure of the date, at least what day is it? Feel yourself physically. Press your thumbs hard against your index fingers, and focus on the physical sensation of that friction.

old: “Only what can be integrated is welcome now. Anything too much can wait. The body may stay safe. The adult self remains present. The inner child does not have to carry this alone.”
new: “I will only allow things through that I can integrate. My body will be kept safe. I will keep my adult self present so my inner child does not have to experience this alone.”

old: Once you’re oriented, choose one intention:
new: Then you can move on to phrases like:

old: “Please show me the next useful truth, symbol, feeling, question, or action — only in the amount I can live well with.”
new: “Show me what I need to know next, in symbols, feelings, questions, actions, etc, but only show me what I can integrate.”

old: Sit upright. Open the eyes. Feel the feet. Let the breath be natural.
new: Sit up, open your eyes, feel your feet on the floor, and breathe naturally

old: Say: “I am not going away. I am coming more fully here.”
new: SAY: I know that I am not going away, but rather that I am coming.

old: Look at one object. Feel the spine.
new: Look at an object and feel your spine

old: “Is this daydream guidance, emotional digestion, or avoidance?”
new: Is this a daydream, are you working something out emotionally, or are you escaping ?

old: “If it is guidance, show me the action inside it. If it is avoidance, bring me gently into the present and show me what I am avoiding.”
new: No matter what the answer is, SAY: Show me what I need to do. If you are escaping, come into the present and show me what I am avoiding.

old: If stillness makes you sleepy, diffuse, or escape-prone, hypnosis can become more alert rather than more relaxed. Keep the eyes open and pair a small repeated hand movement with increasing clarity; stop the movement and notice what remains without trying to disappear inward.
new: If stillness is the problem, make the hypnosis more active. Keep your eyes open and while you do some action with your hand, become more and more clear. Then stop what you are doing and see if it continues

old: “Eyes open. Press thumb and forefinger together gently. Release. Again — clearer, not sleepier. One more time. Now stop the deliberate movement. Notice the first second after the rhythm ends. Is there an echo in the fingers, the breath, the attention, or nowhere at all? Stay upright and work from exactly that level of alertness.”
new: SAY: Keep your eyes open and push your thumb and forefinger together, and when you pull them apart, become more and more clear. Do this several times, and then stop doing it, and see if it continues. Are you more clear? Do your fingers feel different? Do you feel this in any other way, or is there no difference at all. Work at whatever level you are working at now.

old: Place one hand on the heart. Place the other hand on the solar plexus.
new: The next step is to put one hand on over heart and one over solar plexes.

old: Let the heart hand represent the Nurturer. Let the solar plexus hand represent the vulnerable child.
new: The heart, or Nurturer hand, is on top. The lower, or vulnerable child hand is over the solar plexes.

old: Breathe gently.
new: Take a moment to just breathe, and notice the feeling.

old: “Love above. Child below. Adult present.”
new: The words that go along with the motions are "Love above. Child below. Adult here to balance it all."

old: “I send love to the child. I receive the child’s signal. I send love again. I listen again.”
new: As an adult the loop is, I send, I receive, I send again. The words that go along with this are, "I send love to my child. My child is sending me a signal. I send love to my child, as I listen to her signal."

old: Fractionation means returning toward ordinary awareness and then deciding whether to enter absorption again. Used openly, it teaches that trance has a door in both directions. Name the technique before using it; every answer cannot secretly mean “deeper.”
new: This is the process of going back and forth between ordinary awareness and a state of absorption, the nice thing about it is that it can be done openly. Since you are telling them ahead of time what your doing, you need to mention it by name when it’s about to be used. It’s also good to make sure not to stack too many ‘no outs’ as downward, otherwise your subject may think that every answer must lead deeper.

old: “Open the eyes and return toward ordinary awareness. Feel the room and decide whether to stop here. If you choose to continue, close or soften the eyes and notice what changes as attention gathers again. You may stop at either point.”
new: Example of open fractionation: “When i snap your eyes will open and you will come back to ordinary awareness. Once there you will decide if you want to stop or continue. If you decide to continue your eyes will close or soften and you will notice a change, otherwise you will stop right where you are.”

old: “If it is useful, attention may become more gathered. If it is not useful, I remain exactly as awake as I need to be.”
new: Seeing as the information in this thread might be usefull to some people, I figured it might be good to let some attention gather on it. If it's not usefull to ya, know that it leaves me as awake as I need to be and move along. :wink:

old: Choose one simple scene: a room in the heart, a garden, a temple, a fire with the Protector nearby, a clear lake, or a chair where the adult waits. One scene is plenty.
new: Do they have a place they can go to, a scene to paint where they feel safe? (room in the heart, garden, temple, fire with protector, lake, chair with adult etc). Just one is enough.

old: “Who or what needs to speak first?”
new: “Who or what needs to speak first?”

old: “As I wait, I give up the responsibility of making anything happen.
new: Then I wait, giving up any sense of responsibility for what happens.

old: If it is useful, the wise subconscious may let one finger twitch, pulse, lift, warm, tingle, or become subtly noticeable when the inner meeting space is ready.
new: Sometimes, if it's appropriate, my wise subconscious mind will twitch, pulse, lift, warm or tingle a finger so I know it's okay to move into the inner meeting space.

old: I will not force it. I will not fake it. I will simply wait with love and notice.”
new: "I'm not going to force it or fake it. I'll just wait in love and see what happens."

old: A finger may move, a hand may warm, the breath may change, or nothing may happen. None proves truth; at most, something may be listening.
new: Whether something happens, like a finger moving, hand warming or change in the breath, or nothing happens at all, it doesn't really prove anything. Maybe it's listening.

old: Learn a useful induction and the full return below before developing a shortcut. My dad brought two fingers together in a mudra like the OK sign to help himself relax, including while driving. That’s his experience, not a recommendation to enter trance at the wheel. Keep alert calming and inward hypnosis on different cues.
new: Learn a Useful Induction and Full Return First, the reason I suggest not to use a short cut is because you should not be in trance when driving. However, I have seen my dad put two fingers in a mudra (like the ok mudra) to help him relax while driving and that is just his experience, it does not mean that you should. However, it is best to have different triggers for different things, so having a different trigger to be calmly alert while driving, and a different one to go into inward hypnosis is a good idea.

old: Choose a distinctive word, phrase, or optional gesture. During a familiar, welcome hypnotic state, pair it with that receptive way of listening—not peak emotional intensity, a child-state, or a traumatic scene. Give it the meaning you choose:
new: Choose a Unique Word, Phrase or Movement You may want to add a gesture, but it's not necessary. When you are in a familiar and welcome hypnotic state that you like - not at the height of an emotional experience, and not in a child state or with a traumatic scene - start to pair that state with that word, phrase or gesture. You are giving that word, phrase or gesture a meaning that you choose.

old: When I’ve set aside time, settled somewhere appropriate, and deliberately use my cue to begin, I can return to this familiar way of listening. I can change direction or finish.
new: When you are in a place and time where you have set aside time and it is appropriate and you want to deliberately start hypnosis with your short cut, then you will find yourself in that familiar and welcome state, from where you can change the direction of your experience or end the hypnosis.

old: Return fully. On a later suitable occasion, deliberately begin practice and try the cue. Give it time; gradually shorten the longer induction when the shortcut helps, and use the familiar route when it doesn’t. No fixed repetition count, instant depth, or particular sensation is required.
new: Return Fully When at another appropriate time you want to deliberately start practicing hypnosis, use your short cut. You can start to make your longer induction shorter as you find that the short cut works, but if it doesn't work, you can always use the familiar induction. There is no set number of times that you need to do this, or that you need to be instantaneously really deep into hypnosis or experience a particular sensation, it is completely up to you.

old: Check usefulness and selectivity: does it help when chosen, remain absent when unchosen, and leave changing direction and returning workable? It mustn’t become obedience to a narrator, notification, or overheard word. Faster entry doesn’t determine what material you can handle.
new: First, is it useful? Will it be there when you want it to be, not there when you don't want it to be? Can you change your mind about it and get back when you want to? It shouldn't mean you'll do anything you're told, anytime someone tells you, or even if you hear it overheard. Being able to go in faster should not limit what you can work with.

old: Never train, test, or use hypnotic re-entry while driving or doing anything requiring active attention. Open eyes and conditional wording are not safeguards.
new: It's not a good idea to do it while driving or anything where you need to be actively paying attention even if it is open eyed and even if the words are conditional.

old: To retire the cue, stop rehearsing it, remove it from recordings or active app instructions, and return to the familiar induction. State your decision while awake; a cancellation sentence does not prove the association vanished instantly. Persistent unwanted responses or disorientation need qualified help. Any retained cue is for a future, separately chosen session; today’s altered state ends with the return.
new: When you don't want it any more, stop practicing, take it out of any recordings or active apps you're using, go back to a familiar induction and say you're done using it. If you have problems not being able to stop using it or not being able to come back from it easily, get qualified help. The trigger should only be for the next time you decide you want to do a session, it shouldn't keep you out of line today.

old: You can practice the core method without learning one term of Neuro-Linguistic Programming. Read this appendix when you want more precision about imagery, bodily states, rehearsal, and sentence design. NLP is useful when it helps the system listen; it becomes a bag of tricks when technique replaces love, truth, contact, or consent.
new: You don’t have to know the terms to use the system. If you want to brush up on the art of imagery, how imagery is linked to bodily states, how to effectively rehearse new behaviors, how to choose more effective sentences to say to yourself, etc., then you might want to read this appendix. If you don’t know a little bit about NLP, it’s easy to turn NLP into a bag of tricks and forget that love, truth, contact, and consent are essential.

old: Sensory NLP changes the form of an inner experience: image, sound, distance, size, brightness, volume, posture, pressure.
new: When it works, it works on a Sensory Level of NLP: changing where people see or hear an image, the distance or size or brightness, the volume of a sound, the posture of a remembered person, the pressure of an unpleasant sensation.

old: State NLP makes useful states easier to access: warmth, adult presence, courage, steadiness, love, clarity.
new: Second, it works on a State Level of NLP: helping them to access warmth, or a feeling of adult-ness, or courage, or steadiness, or love, or clarity.

old: Strategy NLP rehearses a better response: when this cue appears, the adult does this.
new: Third, it works on a Strategy level of NLP: helping people to practice a new strategy.

old: Language NLP shapes the sentence: pace what is already true, open awareness, presume only safe capacity, link cause and effect carefully, embed invitations, and use de-hypnotic questions when language becomes vague, absolute, manipulative, or grandiose.
new: Fourth, it works on a Language Level of NLP: pacing what is there, opening up people’s awareness, presuming their ability to do something safe, linking cause and effect in new ways, embedding suggestions, or asking de-hypnotic questions to break the effects of vague, absolutes, manipulative, or grandiose language.

old: The Milton Model concerns the architecture of the sentence. Commands such as “Relax now,” “Stop being anxious,” or “Trust me” often make a part brace.
new: It's called the Milton Model and has to do with the architecture of the sentence. When I say "Relax now", or "Stop being anxious", or even "Trust me" a part of me braces against it.

old: Part of the point of indirect language is to get past that reflexive skeptical argument without having to overpower it. The destination can still be deliberate even when the route is subtle.
new: The idea is to use indirect language to get past the part that wants to argue with me, and get to the place I want to go to.

old: Begin with what is already true, lower the pressure, presume only a small safe capacity, and invite one movement:
new: To do that, I start with something I know to be true, and I take the pressure off by presuming the least possible capacity in the person and invite just one movement:

old: “As the body notices the bed beneath it, it may become a little easier to stop holding the whole day alone.”
new: "As the body notices the bed beneath it, it may become a little easier to stop holding the whole day alone."

old: Pace reality. Open awareness. Validate function. Presuppose capacity. Bridge gently. Invite one small movement. Test with the body.
new: That way I pace reality, I open up awareness, I validate the function of what I'm doing, I presuppose the capacity to do what I want, I use a bridge to make the link easier, I invite only one small movement, and I have a way of testing with the body if it's happening.

old: Pacing and leading means stating what is already true before inviting anything new.
new: What is it looks like to pace and lead?

old: “Anxiety is here. The body is activated. A protector is trying to help. And one breath at a time, the adult can start to listen.”
new: Here is an example of pacing and leading for anxiety:

old: The simplest form is a Truth + Invite loop:
new: It can be as simple as: Truth, Invite, Truth, Invite etc.

old: “It is completely true that [current sensation or emotion] is here. It makes sense that my system is reacting by [current protective behavior or thought]. And right alongside that truth, my adult self is here, breathing in this room, ready to listen to whatever comes up next.”
new: “It is completely true that the sensation of _______ (or emotion of _____) is coming up for me right now. It makes complete sense that a part of me is trying to protect me by doing/thinking ________. While that is completely true, another completely true thing is that there is a part of me that is adult, and that is breathing in this room right now, and is willing to listen.

old: Awareness verbs point attention without yelling at it: notice, realize, recognize, sense, feel, wonder, imagine, picture, listen, allow, discover, remember, consider.
new: Awareness Verbs: Notice, realize, recognize, sense, feel, wonder, imagine, picture, listen, allow, discover, remember, consider, etc.

old: “Notice whether the answer comes as an image, a word, a pressure, a warmth, a silence, or a next action.”
new: • Notice how that answer comes for/ to/ within/ for/ inside of/ upon/ into/ amongst/ through/ out of/ out within/ out for/ out upon/ out into/ out amongst/ beyond/ amongst/ through/ out of/ out within/ out for/ out upon/ out into/ out amongst/ within/ for/ to/ inside of/ upon/ into/ amongst/ through/ out of/ out within/ out for/ out upon/ out into/ out amongst/ among/ under/ over/ above/ below/ between/ within and without/ on the inside of and outside of/ on the outside of and inside of/ here and there/ there and here/ through/ out of/ out within/ out for/ out upon/ out into/ out amongst/ within and without/ on the inside of and outside of/ on the outside of and inside of/ here and there/ there and here/

old: Words such as as, while, because, when, after, before, and which means connect one event to another. Use them carefully. A gentle voice doesn’t make a false causal claim true.
new: Be careful with how language link events. Words like “as, while, because, when, after, before, which means” etc are all words that can be used to link events.

old: Too strong: “Because I breathe, the trauma leaves.” Better: “As I breathe, the adult self may become present enough to hear one small piece of what the wound needs.”
new: In general, the problem with the first example is that it’s likely to be inaccurate. It’s unlikely that simply breathing will get rid of the trauma. So while the intention is good, the phrasing is a bit strong. The second example is better because it’s more accurate. As long as the breathing is going on, it’s more likely that the adult version of yourself will be able to get involved in the process and try to help the wounded part of yourself.

old: An embedded invitation places a small direction inside a larger sentence. It should invite a modest inner movement, not hide a demand.
new: What are embedded invitations, and how to use them

old: “And somewhere inside this breath, I can let the adult self listen.”
new: Here is an example of an embedded invitation:

old: “As I sit here, I may allow one small truth to become clear.”
new: Here’s another example of an embedded invitation:

old: “The child does not have to trust me all at once; it can simply notice I am still here.”
new: And yet another embedded invitation for working with inner child parts:

old: Use one when it helps. Ten embedded invitations in a row feel like somebody took a weekend certification.
new: Of course, don’t use ten embedded invitations one after the other, or people will know that’ve just completed a weekend certification course!

old: The Milton Model opens possibility. The Meta Model asks exactly what somebody means. Ethical practice needs both.
new: The Milton Model opens things up. The Meta Model asks for clarification. To be ethical, one needs to use both.

old: “How specifically?” “According to whom?” “Compared to what?” “Always?” “Never?” “What exactly would happen?” “How do I know?” “What evidence would change my mind?”
new: How specifically? According to whom? Compared to what? Always? Never? What exactly would happen? How do I know? What evidence would change my mind?

old: Use Milton Model to soften into the body. Use Meta Model to return to truth.
new: Use the Milton Model to soften into the body. Use the Meta Model to get back to the truth.

old: Fear, craving, fantasy, belief, and memory may have sensory qualities: near or far, bright or dim, loud or quiet, moving or still, heavy or light, inside or outside the body. Work with qualities you actually notice. If none are apparent, skip this tool rather than inventing an image or voice.
new: Are there sensory qualities to the fear, craving, fantasy, belief, or memory? Is it close or far? Bright or dim? Loud or quiet? Moving or static? Heavy or light? Somewhere in your body or outside? If you notice any of these sensory qualities, you can work with them. If not, skip this tool.

old: Ask how the experience is represented. What changes when the image moves two feet back, the voice gets quieter, or the edge becomes less sharp?
new: What if you changed the sensory qualities?

old: “I am not deleting the signal. I am adjusting the volume so I can listen without being overwhelmed.”
new: “It would not be cenzorship to change the sensory qualities. It would only be a way for me to stay in contact with you.”

old: Before moving one imaginary pixel, ask the guard whether that change is acceptable.
new: Ask your guard if it’s ok to change the sensory qualities. For example, you might say:

old: “Would it be okay if we moved this image back just a little, or lowered the volume slightly, purely so my adult self can stay present enough to hear what you need to tell me?”
new: “Would it be ok if I moved the image back a couple of inches? Or turned down the volume a notch? This would enable me to hear you better with my adult mind.”

old: An anchor is a cue connected to a state: a hand on the heart, two fingers touching, a breath, a word, a posture, scent, or song. Find a real state you want easier access to, feel it, and pair the cue while it is clearly present with the phrase, “This is available.” For hypnotic re-entry, choose a usable receptive state rather than peak emotional intensity; follow “A shortcut back into hypnosis” in the main induction section. Keep alert calming and the synchronicity wake-up cue separate.
new: An anchor is a cue that triggers a state. It can be anything - putting your hand on your heart, touching two fingers together, taking a breath, saying a word, a particular posture, scent, song, and so on. Choose something, then find a real state to anchor it to. When you're clearly in the state, apply the anchor and say, 'This is available' . (If you're using the anchor to get back into hypnosis, find a nice useful state - you don't need to be at the peak of emotion, just in a nice receptive state. For more about that, see 'A shortcut back into hypnosis' in the main induction section. ) Make sure you also have a way to bring yourself back to a nice, calming, alert state when you want to be fully awake (see 'synchronicity' above for a way of doing that).

old: People notice a synchronicity and immediately ask what it means. Sometimes that opens insight; sometimes it starts compulsive pattern-hunting. I prefer using the moment of noticing as a wake-up bell. The coincidence doesn’t have to contain a message. It has already captured attention, which is enough.
The cue I give myself is:

“Whenever I notice something that feels like a synchronicity, I wake up inside the state I am in. I feel my body and the room. I remember that the coincidence is not proof of an interpretation. I let attention widen beyond the story my current mood is telling. I ask what is fact, what is interpretation, what needs warmth, what needs protection, and what needs action. I return to the highest perspective I can access without leaving the body, the facts, or ordinary human reality.”
I make room for whatever is genuinely available: objectivity, clarity, ease, peace, freedom, joy, and gratitude. I do not have to manufacture any of them.
Synchronicity noticed → pause → orient → widen → reality-test → listen → choose one loving action.

The cue interrupts identification without erasing the state’s message. A negative state may still contain an inner-child need, a Protector warning, grief, a bodily problem, or a real demand for action.
new: Sometimes when my clients notice a synchronicity they are asking straight way what it means. Sometimes it does give them a very good insight, sometimes it gives them a reason to start obsessing and look for patterns in everything. I am using noticing a synchronicity in a different way. I am using it as a signal to WAKE UP.
It is my cue to:

Whenever I notice a synchronicity, I use it to wake up in whatever state I am in at that moment, feel my body, the room I am in and go to the highest state I can where I can objectively and clearly see the situation I am in from the highest possible perspective, feeling my body and being still within the human reality. From this place I feel whatever feelings, search for the truth of the situation, and if I am in a negative state, I check if there is a message of my Inner Child, Protector, if I need to go through some grieving, if there is a message of my physical body about some problem that needs solving, or if there is a need for me to take some action in this situation. From this place of clarity and peace I am free to choose what to do next and usually I can do at least one thing that comes from a loving place. In this state I am also free and joyful and I feel grateful.
In short it is my cue to: Stop-orient-go wider-reality check-listen-do at least one thing from a loving place.
It enables me to not get into identification, but still hear the message of the state if it is a negative one.

old: Imagine noticing an ordinary, harmless synchronicity.
new: Mentally rehearse: when next synchronicity noticed (even harmless ones count),

old: Feel the moment when attention says, “Whoa.”
new: feel 'whoa' as attention stimulated,

old: Use that opening to feel the feet, body, breath, and room.
new: feel feet/body/breath/room to stimulate re-embodiment,

old: Repeat: “The noticing is my wake-up bell, not proof of a message.”
new: reiterate to yourself "when I notice synchronicity, it is a bell to wake me up, not a message to heed",

old: Ask the Nurturer, Protector, and Leader what each sees.
new: optionally ask Nurturer/Protector/Leader their thoughts,

old: Rehearse returning to a grounded, wider perspective.
new: rehearse further steps to get a more grounded and wide view,

old: End with one small action and the complete waking exit.
new: rehearse what additional action to take, and finally rehearse waking completely,

old: The cue remains self-authored, visible, reversible, and limited to orientation. It can’t authorize a decision, prove an intuition, suppress a warning, or let another person control the response.
new: Mind the caveats : it must be self-authored, obviously under control, reversible, and restricted to just helping orientation. It must not be used for decision-making, intuition, inhibition, or otherwise be under someone else's control.

old: Psychologically, this resembles an implementation intention: an advance “if X, then Y” plan that links a recognizable cue with a chosen response. Gollwitzer’s foundational paper supports the general mechanism. This particular use of synchronicity hasn’t been studied directly.
new: This is a kind of implementation intention , for which there is evidence of efficacy (a good starting point is this paper by Gollwitzer ). Note that this specific application of implementation intentions probably hasn't been studied.

old: The same mechanism creates the risk: rehearsing synchronicity as a cue may make you scan for it. Pattern perception can drift toward false-positive meaning, especially during absorption or destabilization. Research links stronger apophenic pattern detection with false-positive judgments and psychosis-spectrum traits, although ordinary pattern noticing is not itself pathological. See Blain and colleagues and Grant and colleagues.
new: Synchronicity cues, like any cue, run the risk of creating false positives because you are creating an association in your mind by rehearsing it (this is the same mechanism by which synchronicity cues work), and when you are absorbed and/or destabilized, your mind may look for that pattern and interpret it as present when it may not actually be. Research has shown that people that score highly on apophenia (the tendency to perceive meaningful patterns where none exists) also score highly on false positives for patterns that are not present, and also score highly on traits on the psychosis spectrum (Blain et al., Grant et al.).

old: Deactivate the cue if it increases compulsive scanning, sleeplessness, anxiety, certainty that random events are personally directed messages, or difficulty distinguishing observation from interpretation.
new: If you feel that synchronicity cues are creating false positives (you find yourself compelled to scan your environment for them, you are unable to sleep, you are anxious, you feel that random events are occurring to communicate something to you specifically, you find yourself unable to tell if they are real or not, etc.), you should deactivate them.

old: To retire it, stop rehearsing it and say while fully awake: “Synchronicity is no longer a cue. I release this association and return coincidence to ordinary uncertainty.” Remove it from the written cue list and stop rehearsing it. The statement expresses your decision; it does not prove the association has vanished immediately.
new: You can do this by simply ceasing to rehearse them, and saying, while fully awake, “Synchronicity is no longer to be used as a cue, and I let it go.” Also remove it from your list of cues so that you stop rehearsing it.

old: Dishonest reframing declares that the problem was secretly good all along. I prefer questions that widen meaning without lying:
“What else might be true?” “What is this part trying to do for me?” “What would the Nurturer, the Protector, and the Leader each say about this?”
new: When I reframe something that is dishonest with myself in the process, I’m no better off than before, so I have to be honest when I reframe. To reframe in a helpful way is to ask myself a series of questions like: “What else could be true here?” or “What is this part trying to do for me?” or “How would my Nurturer reframe this?” or “How would my Protector reframe this?” or “How would my Leader reframe this?” and so on.

old: First: what do I feel from inside myself? Second: if I sit inside the other person, what might they be feeling or protecting? Third: if I watched this from across the room, what would I notice? Fourth: from the universal heart, what serves truth, love, boundaries, and the good of everyone involved?
new: 1. How do I feel about this from inside myself? 2. If I were inside of this other person (or tree, or dog or whatever is not-you), how might I feel? 3. If I were across the room watching this, what would I see? 4. From the universal heart, what might be true, loving, clear about boundaries, and good for everyone involved?

old: Don’t use perceptual positions to excuse harm. Use them to escape the prison of one angle.
new: Yes, it’s possible to use these positions to let yourself off the hook. It’s also possible to use them to get off the hook! Use them to see the truth from more than one angle. They’re a great way to get out of a prison of perception.

old: Classic NLP uses the Swish to replace an old self-image with a new one. Done mechanically, it can feel like an inner eviction. Here, the old pattern stays visible, the new possibility stands beside it, and I notice the body’s response while comparing what each future would actually require.
new: In classic NLP, one of the uses of the Swish was to replace an old image of yourself with a new, better one. Some people find that method jarring. So here is a gentler way to do it, leaving the old pattern in place, but letting it sit side by side with a new pattern, so that the client can feel, in their body, which one they want to pursue, and see what it would take to get there.

old: To talk myself out of a real signal.
To override fear before asking what the fear protects.
To recover memories.
To manipulate anyone else.
To convince myself an intuition is true.
To erase pain, hunger, grief, anger, or a medical symptom.
While panicking, destabilized, manic, psychosis-like, chemically overwhelmed, or too dissociated to reality-test.
To make another person’s no feel like resistance.
To make someone feel spiritually inferior for disagreeing.
To hide a command inside soft language.
To create urgency where time is needed.
To bypass consent by calling something “subconscious agreement.”
To use trance, fatigue, attraction, shame, grief, or altered states to get compliance.
new: To “explain away” a true signal that is coming through
To override any fear signals that are present
To bring up memories, or to manipulate others
To believe something to be “true” within yourself
To remove discomfort such as: pain, hunger, sadness, anger, or medical symptoms
While in a state of panic, destabilization, mania, psychosis-like symptoms, chemical overload, or other dissociative states that are removing connection to reality for the purpose of
Making someone feel that saying “No” is bad
Making someone feel inferior in a spiritual way
Making someone feel a command, using “soft language”
To create a false urgency within someone, when they need time
To bypass actual consent by suggesting that the person is “subconsciously” consenting
To manipulate someone by using their trance, tiredness, attraction, shame, grief, or other altered state to gain compliance

old: Induce or contain. Gather attention, or stabilize first if you are already wide open.
new: Induce or contain (if client already in altered state).

old: Ask permission. Is it useful to work with this image, feeling, or pattern today?
new: Ask permission to work with this part.

old: Represent the pattern. How does this show up — image, voice, sensation, posture, distance, size, color, movement?
new: Help client accurately represent this pattern. What does it look like? Where? How big? How close? What color? How does it move?

old: Ask what it protects. What is this trying to do for me?
new: Ask what it is trying to do for the client.

old: Adjust the form, gently. Move it back, lower the volume, add space, change posture, slow the scene.
new: Have client make adaptive changes in the pattern (move it further away, turn down the volume, change body posture, slow it down, etc.).

old: Bring in the three adults. Nurturer warms, Protector makes it safe, Leader points a direction.
new: Introduce the three new adults (Nurturer, Protector and Leader) and have them interact with the pattern in new ways.

old: Anchor the useful state. Heart, fingers, breath, posture.
new: Have client anchor the new state (heart, fingers, breath, body posture, etc.).

old: Future pace. If the old cue shows up, what is the smallest new action?
new: Have client future pace into a situation where this pattern used to be triggered, but now he/she will perform a new behavior.

old: Check the fit and the evidence. What changes in the body? Is the response kind and doable? What supports the interpretation beyond how it feels?
new: Test and retest to ensure that new pattern is useful and that you have supporting evidence for your interpretation of the situation.

old: Exit and act. Come back to the room. Do one ordinary thing.
new: Help client exit altered state and perform a normal behavior.
